meta.description: Not Mother Teresa. The line is Kent M. Keith's 1968 “Paradoxical Commandments” — and even ‘forgive them anyway’ is a later paraphrase of his ‘love them anyway.’
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'People are often unreasonable, illogical and self-centered; forgive them anyway'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Mother Teresa. It's Kent M. Keith's 1968 Paradoxical Commandments, misattributed via a sign at her Calcutta children's home.

answer.label: Not Mother Teresa — actually Kent M. Keith
answer.authorDates: b. 1949 · American writer & former student leader
answer.sourceLine: The line is the opening of Kent M. Keith’s “The Paradoxical Commandments,” written in 1968 for a student-leadership booklet at Harvard. Keith’s original reads “People are illogical, unreasonable, and self-centered. Love them anyway” — the popular “forgive them anyway” form is a later paraphrase. It reached Mother Teresa’s name because a version hung on a wall at her Calcutta children’s home and was reprinted in a 1995 book about her; she did not write it.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: People are illogical, unreasonable, and self-centered. Love them anyway.
trail: Kent M. Keith wrote the ten “Paradoxical Commandments” in 1968 for a student-leadership booklet; his original opening line is “People are illogical, unreasonable, and self-centered. Love them anyway” (paradoxicalcommandments.com).

Quote Investigator traces the Mother Teresa misattribution to a 1995 book, A Simple Path (compiled by Lucinda Vardey), which printed the lines under “Anyway” with a note that they came “from a sign on the wall of Shishu Bhavan, the children’s home in Calcutta.”
Wikiquote files the “Anyway” poem under Misattributed, calling it “a variant or paraphrase of The Paradoxical Commandments, by Kent M. Keith.”
source.excerptNote: Keith’s original 1968 first commandment. The widely shared “People are often unreasonable, illogical and self-centered; forgive them anyway” is a reworded later variant of this line.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: “Do Good Anyway” — the Paradoxical Commandments

source.rightsNote: “The Paradoxical Commandments” was written by Kent M. Keith in 1968 and carries his copyright (renewed 2001), so it is in copyright in the United States. The anonymous “forgive them anyway” rewording is a derivative variant of that copyrighted work, not a separately sourced older text.

author.name: Kent M. Keith
author.heading: Kent M. Keith
author.metaLine: b. 1949 · American author, lawyer & former student leader
author.bio: Kent M. Keith wrote “The Paradoxical Commandments” in 1968 as a Harvard sophomore, for a booklet aimed at student-council leaders. The list circulated for decades — often anonymously or misattributed — before Keith rediscovered its fame and reclaimed authorship in his 2001 book Anyway. He has since written and spoken widely on ethical leadership and finding personal meaning.

misattribution.heading: How Mother Teresa got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most durable inspirational misattributions online. The words are Kent M. Keith’s, and even the familiar “forgive them anyway” wording is a paraphrase of what he actually wrote.

items.why: A version of Keith’s commandments hung on a wall at Shishu Bhavan, her Calcutta children’s home, and was reprinted in the 1995 book A Simple Path with only a “sign on the wall” note — so readers assumed she authored it (Quote Investigator).

Keith’s original 1968 line is “People are illogical, unreasonable, and self-centered. Love them anyway.” The “often… forgive them anyway” form is a later, altered variant (paradoxicalcommandments.com).

items.who: Dempsey Byrd, Howard Ferguson & E. T. Gurney
items.why: Before Mother Teresa, Quote Investigator documents the lines being credited to a school administrator (1972), a wrestling coach (1981), and a name in an Ann Landers column (1983) — a pattern of anonymous reprinting (QI).

misattribution.truthLine: The author is Kent M. Keith, who wrote “The Paradoxical Commandments” in 1968 — confirmed by Quote Investigator and Wikiquote.

context.heading: Why the mix-up stuck
lead: Mother Teresa was a natural magnet for the poem: it preaches selfless perseverance, and it literally hung on a wall in one of her homes. Once a compiler printed it in a book about her with nothing but a “sign on the wall” note, the leap from “displayed by Mother Teresa” to “written by Mother Teresa” happened fast and never reversed.

Keith, meanwhile, had written the lines as a 19-year-old and largely lost track of them. He only learned they had become world-famous — under other people’s names — decades later, and reclaimed them in his 2001 book Anyway.
context.pull: She hung it on a wall; the internet decided she wrote it.
